three impure klipos and klipas nogah
Shechinah in a gathering of ten
Chanukah and Purim as galus Yamim Tovim
chesed and gevurah in the Merkava

title.en: Tumah imitates kedusha like a monkey

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that tumah mimics kedusha: the kuf imitates the hei of Hashem's Name, and Achashverosh's feast imitated the Beis HaMikdash. The difference is that kedusha is batel to Hashem while tumah stands on its own, cut off from its supply; yet every Yid is inwardly batel.

title.en: Torah with yiras Shamayim and the ten

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Shechinah rests on one who learns Torah, provided he learns with yiras Shamayim, comparing Torah without it to an empty capsule or an unplugged radio. He then shows that ten Yidden always have the Shechinah, and that even the ten spies, from whom davar shebikdusha is learned, had it because inwardly they were tzaddikim.

title.en: Life from the back side, renewed each moment

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that whatever is not batel is a separate entity, yet it exists only through Hashem's word, contracted countless times into a tiny spark given from the 'back side'. He stresses that creation is not a historical fact but happens anew every moment.

title.en: The spark in exile and Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Tanya's chiddush that even the energy of a rasha doing an aveirah is created at that moment from Hashem, a tiny spark that is in exile. He connects this to Chanukah, when the Shechinah comes below ten tefachim, and says the avodah of a Yid is to redeem such sparks.

title.en: A world mostly evil; Shabbos and Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that this world is the world of klipos, mostly evil, as seen in nature. On Shabbos and Yom Tov a Yid rises above it, since melachah is a curse; on Chanukah and Purim, days when work is permitted, kedusha comes down to him. He ties this to Eliezer leaving the curse for blessing and to Shabbos Mevarchim Kislev.

title.en: Three impure klipos and the Merkava

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the lower level of klipos, the three impure klipos, cannot be elevated until Moshiach. He brings the four klipos Yechezkel passed on the way to the Merkava, explains why the Ba'al HaTanya does not spell them all out, and shows from the lion and eagle of the Merkava how gevurah becomes impure on its way down. An audience question on mentioning resha'im follows.

title.en: What draws life from the impure klipos

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the levels of creation, domem, tzome'ach, chai and medaber, and explains that the existence of non-kosher animals and of forbidden growths like orlah and kilai hakerem comes from the three impure klipos, which is why they are forbidden from their inception. He notes that the Tanya does not list domem and begins to explain why.

title.en: Chesed over din: male and female

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in kedusha the male, chesed, is meant to dominate the female, din, and digresses to criticize the modern equality movement, contrasting it with the harmony of Jewish homes. He connects this to Esav's wives going first and to giving the right side precedence over the left.

title.en: The Or HaChaim's dream and the seven nations

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Or HaChaim's dream of a male and a female dog, showing that in the sitra achra the female is stronger. He maps the seven nations onto the middos, explains that the Girgashi is malchus and left voluntarily, which is why domem is batel and not listed, and sums up the perek: ten crowns of tumah exist mainly in this world, while kedusha is batel to Hashem.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Shabbos Shirah

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Shabbos Shirah, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem made a Jew's eating into mitzvos that bring kedushah into his body, and that the seudah of a bris is a seudah of geulah, bound up with Eliyahu Hanavi and Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with the passuk of the manna, 'bread from heaven', and explains that a person's food becomes his life and part of his flesh and blood; eating matzah means taking geulah into oneself. Since all of life depends on eating, Hashem, wishing to give Jews merit, made mitzvos of every meal: washing, hamotzi, the brachos after it, mayim rishonim and acharonim. The Torah is eternal, so every meal is still bread from heaven, and all a Jew's Torah, tefillah and chessed draw their strength from it. He brings the Ba'al HaTurim that a passuk about the manna holds all the letters of the alef-beis. Shabbos and every Yom Tov have their own foods. A bris removes the orlah and is a foretaste of geulah, so Eliyahu Hanavi comes, and its seudah is a seudah of geulah that one may not refuse. He closes on Shabbos Shirah and brachos.

en: Food becomes a person's life and part of his flesh and blood, so eating matzah means taking geulah into oneself.
Because all of life depends on eating, Hashem made mitzvos of every meal: washing, hamotzi, the brachos after eating, mayim rishonim and mayim acharonim.
Since the Torah is eternal, every meal today is also 'bread from heaven', and all of a Jew's words of Torah, tefillah and chessed draw their life from his eating.
Shabbos and every Yom Tov, even Chanukah and Purim, have their own foods, halachos and customs.
A bris is a foretaste of the days of Moshiach, so Eliyahu Hanavi comes to it and its seudah is a seudah of geulah.
The Mashgiach explains through this why the poskim say one should not refuse an invitation to a bris seudah: refusing it is refusing geulah.

candidateTopics: the manna as bread from heaven

title.en: Eating as mitzvah and bread from heaven

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains from the manna and from matzah that food becomes a person's life, that Hashem made mitzvos of every meal, and that every meal is bread from heaven. He brings the Ba'al HaTurim on the letters of the alef-beis in a passuk of the manna, and the special foods of Shabbos and Yom Tov.

title.en: The bris seudah as a seudah of geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a bris removes the orlah and is a foretaste of geulah, which is why Eliyahu Hanavi comes and why one should not refuse its seudah. He says the revelation of Eliyahu depends on the home, connects the bris to Shabbos Shirah, and blesses the child and family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Beshalach, the Mashgiach contrasts the hardened heart that brought the plagues on Egypt with the circumcision of the heart that the bris of the flesh awakens in Heaven.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the plagues of Egypt, which were made heavier by an even harsher blow, the hardening of the heart, while from all of it came a great salvation for the Jews. Against that hardened heart he sets the heart a Jew asks for: one inclined to love and fear of Heaven and ready to fulfill the will of the Ribono shel Olam. The parshiyos of this time, and Beshalach in particular, speak of that hardening, and since the Torah is a Torah of life, reading them in their week gives strength to work against it. These are also the weeks of Shovavim, set aside for this. The bris of the flesh, he explains, awakens in Heaven the verse that Hashem will circumcise the heart, removing its covering so that fear of Heaven can enter. He closes with blessings that the child grow into an upright Jew and bring nachas to his family and to all of Klal Yisrael.

en: The plagues of Egypt were compounded by a harsher blow, the hardening of the heart, and from all of it came a great salvation for the Jews.
A Jew asks for a heart inclined to love and fear of Heaven and ready to do the will of the Ribono shel Olam, the opposite of a hardened heart.
Because the Torah is a Torah of life, the week in which Parshas Beshalach is read gives strength to work against hardness of heart.
The bris of the flesh awakens in Heaven the circumcision of the heart, as in the verse that Hashem will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring.
The Mashgiach blesses the child to grow into an upright Jew and bring nachas to his parents, grandparents and all of Klal Yisrael.

candidateTopics: torah as a torah of life

title.en: Hardened heart and circumcised heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the hardened heart of the Egypt parshiyos with the heart that serves Hashem, ties the bris in the week of Beshalach and Shovavim to the verse that Hashem will circumcise the heart, and closes with blessings for the child.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shabbos Shirah usually brings only a temporary, 'feminine' salvation, but a bris in its week awakens the light of Moshiach and draws down true lights of the final redemption, as on Shevi'i shel Pesach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach compares the two days on which the song at the Sea is read: Shevi'i shel Pesach, with the haftarah of Dovid's song, and Shabbos Shirah, with the haftarah of Devorah's song. The reading awakens the time, so on Shevi'i shel Pesach, the day of the miracle itself, great lights of redemption come down, reaching to the third Beis HaMikdash. On Shabbos Shirah there is only the reading, and only a semblance of those lights. He brings Chazal that the song at the Sea is called by a feminine name, while the song of the future is masculine: every redemption until the last was followed by more troubles, like a woman who gives birth again and again, but the last will be once and for all. This is why Devorah's song ends with forty years of quiet, while Dovid's ends with kindness to his anointed forever. Since a bris awakens the aspect of Moshiach, a bris in the week of Shabbos Shirah can draw true lights of redemption, and he blesses the child accordingly.

en: Reading the account of a miracle awakens the same lights that came down at the time of the miracle.
On Shevi'i shel Pesach the day of the miracle and the reading join and bring great lights of redemption; on Shabbos Shirah there is only the reading, and only a semblance of those lights.
All redemptions before the last were 'feminine', followed again by troubles, while the final redemption will be 'masculine', once and for all.
This is reflected in the endings of the two haftaros: Devorah's song ends with forty years of quiet, while Dovid's song ends with salvation for his offspring forever.
At a bris the aspect of Moshiach is awakened, so a bris in the week of Shabbos Shirah can draw true lights of redemption as on Shevi'i shel Pesach.

title.en: Shevi'i shel Pesach, Shabbos Shirah, and the 'feminine' song

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the reading of the song at the Sea awakens its lights, fully on Shevi'i shel Pesach and only in part on Shabbos Shirah, and brings Chazal that past redemptions were 'feminine' and temporary, while the final one will be 'masculine' and permanent.

title.en: The two haftaros and the bris that brings redemption

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the difference in the endings of the haftaros of Shevi'i shel Pesach and Shabbos Shirah, then explains that a bris awakens the aspect of Moshiach, so a bris in this week draws true lights of redemption, and closes with a blessing for the child.

catalogTitle: ביאור קליפת נוגה - “קדושים תהיו” - כנגד פריעה. (ישמעאל ומצוות מילה)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains klipas nogah, the middle layer that a Jew can elevate by using permitted things l'shem shamayim, and shows the same pattern in milah and priyah, which he connects to Yishmael's claim on Eretz Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the three wholly impure klipos, which can never be elevated, with klipas nogah, a scale that tips toward kedushah or tumah depending on intent. Kosher food is nogah: eaten l'shem shamayim it rises like a korban, eaten in excess it sinks. Citing the Ramban on 'kedoshim tihyu' and a psychologist's view that enjoyment is a real human need, he sets two conditions: no excess, and l'shem shamayim. Reading Tanya chapter seven, he explains that nogah is all good above but mixed below, and that meat and wine taken for an expanded mind for Torah, or for oneg Shabbos, are elevated. He finds the same rule in milah, where three layers are cut off and the fourth, priyah, is pulled up. This leads to Yishmael's 'empty' milah, Chevron as the place of milah, Shechem as the place of priyah, and the Shaagas Aryeh's chiddush that Bnei Yishmael are not obligated in priyah.

en: The three impure klipos can never be elevated, while klipas nogah is like a scale that tips toward kedushah or tumah depending on how it is used.
Kosher food eaten l'shem shamayim rises like a korban; eaten without need it is drawn into tumah until teshuvah lifts it.
Enjoyment is a real human need, but it must not be in excess and must be for the sake of serving Hashem.
Nogah is entirely good above but mixed with bad in this world; using it for good separates the good and raises it.
In milah the three layers cut off correspond to the three impure klipos, and priyah, the fourth layer pulled upward, corresponds to klipas nogah.
Bnei Yishmael, whose body stems from the three impure klipos, can repair only through milah and have no share in priyah, which corresponds to nogah.

title.en: Two extremes and the middle of klipas nogah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the previous chapters: through mitzvos a person becomes a seat for kedushah, through aveiros a seat for the three wholly impure klipos. He introduces klipas nogah as a middle layer, like a scale that can tip either way, unlike forbidden food, which can never be elevated.

title.en: Kosher food tips up or down; the Ramban on kedoshim tihyu

summary.en: Kosher food, bound up with the body, is klipas nogah: eaten l'shem shamayim it rises like a korban, eaten without need it is drawn into tumah until teshuvah lifts it again, while the harm of forbidden food stays even after teshuvah. He brings the Ramban on 'kedoshim tihyu' that even permitted pleasures must be sanctified, or a person becomes a degenerate with the Torah's license.

title.en: Why a person needs enjoyment, and its limits

summary.en: The Mashgiach relates a psychologist's point that a person fed without tasting would break down, so enjoyment is a real need; but it must not be in excess and must be l'shem shamayim. A cookie to perk up one's learning is fine, a cookie because of a pleasant aroma is excess, and he cites his rebbe Rav Mendlowitz on a Midrash about the Leviasan's belly being in America.

title.en: Tanya ch. 7: the vital soul and permitted things

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of chapter seven: the vital soul of a Jew, the life of kosher animals, birds and fish, permitted produce, and permitted deeds and words draw from klipas nogah, not from the three impure klipos. He illustrates with someone talking about a ball game, which is no aveirah, and explains that nogah in its source above, the brightness around Hashem in Yechezkel, is entirely good.

title.en: Elevating nogah: meat, wine and oneg Shabbos

summary.en: In this world nogah is a mixture of good and bad on the borderline between the impure klipos and kedushah; used for good, the good separates and rises. He brings the example of fat meat and fragrant wine taken to gain an expanded mind for Torah, citing Rava, and distinguishes this preparation for a mitzvah from oneg Shabbos and Yom Tov, which is a mitzvah in itself.

title.en: Milah and priyah; Yishmael's empty milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the same rule in milah: the three layers cut off correspond to the three impure klipos, while the thin fourth layer of priyah is pulled up and elevated, like klipas nogah, and similarly the fourth year of a newly planted tree. He turns to Bnei Yishmael, circumcised at thirteen, and the Zohar that Eretz Yisrael was given to them for their empty milah and stays barren in their hands; the Gemara calls its renewed fruitfulness the clearest sign of the geulah.

title.en: Every place in Eretz Yisrael is a halachah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Temurah about the halachos forgotten after Moshe Rabbeinu's passing, which Osniel ben Kenaz restored through his pilpul, and an explanation that every place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a part of the Torah. Kiryas Sefer held those halachos, so mastering them let Osniel conquer the place; the plain meaning and the drash are both true.

title.en: Chevron, the place of milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chevron is the territory of the mitzvah of milah, Avraham Avinu's own mitzvah, which is why he bought the Me'aras HaMachpelah with money. The Arabs, who claim Eretz Yisrael through their milah, fight hardest over Chevron, but he says Hashem will shake them out of the land like a sheet, since their milah is only an imitation.

title.en: The imitation and the genuine son of Avraham

summary.en: Responding to a listener, the Mashgiach brings the Ba'al HaTurim on the passage of Yishmael's end followed by the offspring of Yitzchak ben Avraham: Yishmael claims to be the son of Avraham, while Yitzchak is the genuine one. He says each generation has a rasha who embodies Yishmael's accusation, in his time Arafat, whose name he shows equals 'Yishmael ben Avraham' in gematria.

title.en: Shaagas Aryeh: milah without priyah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Shaagas Aryeh's chiddush that Bnei Yishmael are obligated only in milah, not priyah, and confirms it from Kabbalah: their body stems from the three impure klipos, so they cannot repair nogah. He adds a gematria on 'tachlis', a Midrash he heard from Rav Mendlowitz, and the halachah that a gentile may bring only an olah, not a shelamim, since only a Jew can make eating into avodah.

title.en: Shechem, the place of priyah, and the closing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that priyah was given in Yehoshua's time, and Yehoshua comes from Yosef, whose purchased portion is Shechem, so Shechem is the place of priyah as Chevron is the place of milah. He closes that the work of klipas nogah is harnessing bodily pleasure to Hashem's will, like fourth-year fruit, and ends with a story of a seminary professor who spent his whole hour on the root of one word.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Yisro, the Mashgiach shows that Yisro's meal with the elders was a seudas bris that opened him to Torah, and that Hashem takes up the cause of those who come late, so a bris delayed for the child's health is dear and brings healing.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the verse that Aharon and the elders ate bread with Yisro, explaining that this was a seudas bris, since Yisro had converted. Right after it, the next day, Yisro already added a parsha to the Torah, for Torah enters only one who is circumcised, as Chazal relate about Onkelos. He blesses the child, from a family of Torah, to grow into a talmid chacham. In a second talk he brings a Midrash, cited by the Be'er Mayim Chaim, that Amalek attacked those left outside the Clouds of Glory because they had fallen behind, and Hashem fights for them. Yisro too came late, after the counting of the Omer had begun, and feared he would not be accepted, but Hashem draws the latecomer close. So a bris delayed for the child's health is no lesser bris: it shows how precious a Jew's body is to Hashem and draws down healing for all Jews.

en: The meal at which Aharon and the elders ate with Yisro was a seudas bris, held because Yisro had converted.
Torah does not enter one who is uncircumcised, so right after his bris Yisro merited to add a parsha to the Torah.
Amalek could attack only those who had fallen behind and were left outside the Clouds of Glory, and Moshe sent Yehoshua to fight for them.
Yisro, who came after the counting of the Omer had begun, feared he would not be accepted, but Hashem draws close the one who comes late.
A bris delayed for the child's health is not a lesser bris; it arouses in Heaven the importance of a Jew's body and draws down healing.

title.en: Yisro's seudas bris and the Torah that followed

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the meal of Aharon and the elders with Yisro was a seudas bris, after which Yisro immediately added a parsha to the Torah, since Torah enters only one who is circumcised, and blesses the child, from a family of Torah, to become a talmid chacham.

title.en: Amalek, the latecomers, and Yisro

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a Midrash cited by the Be'er Mayim Chaim that Amalek attacked those who had fallen behind outside the Clouds of Glory and Hashem fights for them, and explains that Yisro, who came late, feared rejection but was drawn close.

title.en: A delayed bris and the worth of a Jew's body

summary.en: The Mashgiach addresses a bris held late, for the child's health: one might think it a lesser bris, but it shows how precious a Jew's body is to Hashem and draws down healing for all Jews; he closes with blessings.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in Adar, the Mashgiach explains with the Chasam Sofer that a Jew's true birth is his bris, which is why Haman knew Moshe Rabbeinu's day of death but not his day of birth.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Haman's joy when the lot fell on Adar: he knew Moshe Rabbeinu died in that month but not that he was born in it. Everyone asks why Haman could work out the one date and not the other. The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer's answer: the main birth of a Jewish child is at his bris, when he enters kedushah and gains his bond with Torah, mitzvos and the Ribono shel Olam. Haman counted Moshe's birth from an expected bris on the eighth day, not knowing that Moshe was born already circumcised, so his true birth was on the day he was born. The Mashgiach then notes that the days around a birthday share in it, so a bris held now in Adar, close to the day of Moshe Rabbeinu's birth and in a month of good fortune, is especially auspicious. He closes with blessings for the child and the family.

en: Haman rejoiced that the lot fell on Adar because he knew Moshe Rabbeinu died in it, but he did not know Moshe was also born in it.
According to the Chasam Sofer, the main birth of a Jewish child is at his bris, when he enters kedushah.
Moshe Rabbeinu was born circumcised, so his bris and his birth were on the same day, which Haman did not know.
The days just before and after a birthday share in it, so a bris now in Adar is close to the day of Moshe Rabbeinu's birth.

title.en: The bris as a Jew's true birth

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Haman knew the date of Moshe Rabbeinu's death but not of his birth, and answers with the Chasam Sofer that a Jew's true birth is his bris and Moshe was born circumcised. He ties the present bris in Adar to Moshe Rabbeinu's birth and closes with blessings for the family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris around Purim, the Mashgiach explains that Eliyahu, the angel of the bris, appears in the Megillah as Charvona at Haman's downfall, because every bris removes the orlah of the world, and that the true joy of 'sasson' is milah, which lifts a Jew above nature.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Charvona's words about the gallows and the Midrash that Charvona was Eliyahu HaNavi, and asks why Eliyahu appears in the Megillah only there and not by name. He explains that Eliyahu is the angel of the bris, a role he earned when he removed the orlah in the incident of Zimri and was given 'My covenant of peace'. Every bris removes orlah and reveals kedushah throughout creation, until all of it is gone and Moshiach is revealed. When Haman, the orlah of creation, was hanged, Eliyahu came as the angel of the bris. The Mashgiach then brings the Chasam Sofer on the word Megillah and the drashah that 'sasson' is milah: with the Rambam's explanation that milah weakens nature, he explains that true joy is not worldly pleasure but rising above nature in a bond with the Ribono shel Olam. He closes with blessings for the child and for the final redemption.

en: According to the Midrash, Charvona in the Megillah was Eliyahu HaNavi, who comes as the angel of the bris.
Eliyahu became the angel of the bris when he removed the orlah in the incident of Zimri and was given Hashem's covenant of peace.
Every bris removes some of the orlah of the world and reveals kedushah, until all of it is removed and Moshiach is revealed.
Haman's hanging was a removal of the orlah of creation, so Eliyahu, the angel of the bris, appears there.
Chazal's 'sasson is milah' means that true joy comes from milah, which weakens a person's nature and binds him to Hashem, not from passing worldly pleasures.

removing the orlah of the world

title.en: Charvona, Eliyahu and the angel of the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Charvona was Eliyahu HaNavi and asks why he appears only there in the Megillah. He explains that Eliyahu is the angel of the bris since the incident of Zimri, that every bris removes orlah from creation, and that Haman's hanging was such a removal; Adar is a time of covenant.

title.en: Sasson is milah: true joy above nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer on the word Megillah and the drashah that 'sasson' is milah, and with the Rambam that milah weakens nature he explains that true joy is rising above worldly pleasures to a bond with the Ribono shel Olam. He closes with blessings for the child and for the redemption.

catalogTitle: קליפת נוגה בארבע יסודות. חילוק בין תיקון חטא דקליפת נוגה וחטא דשלש קליפות הטמאות.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 7, the Mashgiach explains how the permitted pleasures of kelipas nogah can be raised back to kedushah, why forbidden things stay bound until the final redemption, and how teshuvah from love turns even sins into merits.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues Tanya chapter 7. After the example of a light word said to lift the mood for learning, he turns to one who eats meat and drinks wine for pleasure alone. Pleasure comes from the element of water; such eating draws the food down into kelipas nogah. Because kosher food is 'heter', untied, it rises again when its energy is used for avodas Hashem, while forbidden food is 'asur', tied to the three impure kelipos. He explains that a person's possessions are sparks of his own soul, placed with him by hashgacha pratis, and why later generations added chumros. Even raised, permitted indulgence leaves a mark that the beating of the grave removes, while forbidden food needs Gehinnom or the end of death itself. He discusses samples of that future purification, and closes with teshuvah from love, which raises the baal teshuvah above the tzaddik and turns sins into merits.

en: Pleasure derives from the element of water, and eating meat or drinking wine only for pleasure draws them down into kelipas nogah.
Kosher food eaten for pleasure can rise back to kedushah when its energy is later used for avodas Hashem, because 'heter' means untied; forbidden food is 'asur', tied to the impure kelipos.
Everything a person owns holds sparks of his own soul, brought to him by hashgacha pratis, and using it for Heaven's sake redeems them.

Even after permitted indulgence is raised, a mark remains in the body; it is cleansed by the beating of the grave, while what is absorbed from forbidden food needs Gehinnom or the end of death in the future.
Teshuvah from great love reaches the level of the future redemption and can release even forbidden things; a baal teshuvah's sins become merits because they fueled his return.

sparks of the soul in possessions

title.en: Review, and a light word for a good purpose

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews that deeds in thought, speech and action can tilt to kedushah or to the impure kelipos, then explains the Tanya's example of saying something humorous to lighten the mood so that one can learn and daven better.

title.en: The four elements and the pleasure of water

summary.en: The Mashgiach turns to those who eat meat and drink wine only to satisfy desire. He explains the four elements, that every pleasure comes from the element of water, and why wine is especially dangerous, bringing a remark on the words of Kiddush.

title.en: Heter is untied, issur is bound

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that kosher meat and wine eaten for desire fall into kelipas nogah but rise back when he uses their energy for avodas Hashem, because a permitted thing is 'untied'; forbidden food stays bound and its energy cannot raise Torah.

title.en: Sparks of the soul in one's possessions

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that by exact hashgacha pratis every possession, his yarmulke, his bread, his home, carries sparks related to his soul, which he redeems by using them for Heaven's sake. He illustrates with a lost yarmulke, a broken glass and a loaf of bread, and brings the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Rambam on health.

title.en: Why later generations added chumros

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Rema forbids things the Gemara permits. He explains that borderline items could once be refined by great souls through their avodah and brachos, but later poskim saw that such things are now bound by thin strings that this generation cannot cut.

title.en: The mark that remains in the body

summary.en: Reading the Tanya that a mark of the indulgence remains in the body, the Mashgiach compares it to a stain left on a shirt, connects it to Rashi on a tzaddik leaving a mark, explains why fervent young people can grow coarse with age, and brings that the beating of the grave removes this mark.

title.en: Dust and stains: the grave, Gehinnom and the end of death

summary.en: With the mashal of a dusty mattress beaten clean versus a cloth that needs hot water, the Mashgiach explains that permitted indulgence is removed by the beating of the grave and forbidden pleasure by Gehinnom, while what is fully bound rises only when death is swallowed up forever.

title.en: Samples of the future purification

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the question how Moshe Rabbeinu could use Egyptian animals that had been worshipped as korbanos, and the Satmar Rav's answer that Yetzias Mitzrayim was a local sample of the future end of tumah. He adds the Rema on adorning the Seder table with pledged vessels and explains bitul b'shishim as a case Hashem arranges, which a person may not do himself.

title.en: Teshuvah from love: a private redemption

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya that teshuvah from great love, with a thirst like parched land, releases even forbidden things, a private sample of the future redemption. He brings that baalei teshuvah stand where complete tzaddikim cannot, and the Zohar's mashal of a bird escaping from a hand.

title.en: Sins become merits

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the sin itself caused the baal teshuvah's higher level, so it is rectified at its root and becomes a merit, as Chazal say. He ends with a question on Rashi about a tzaddik son of a rasha and a tzaddik son of a tzaddik.

oneLiner.en: At a bris around Purim, the Mashgiach explains that milah, done on a child without understanding, expresses the hidden point of Avraham Avinu in every Jew that is above intellect, the same point revealed on Purim 'until one does not know'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the verse that the Jews had light, gladness, joy and honor, and the Gemara's reading that joy is milah and honor is tefillin. Purim, he says, reveals the hidden root in every Jew: a Jew has free choice, but he also has a pintele Yid, a point from the Avos that cannot be extinguished, which Hashem guards as 'Magen Avraham'. This point is above intellect, which is why even simple Jews give their lives for emunah, and why on Purim Jews reach 'until one does not know'. Milah is the bris of Avraham Avinu, the first Jew, and so it is done on a child who has no understanding: its depth is above daas. Tefillin, in contrast, is a mitzvah of daas. Together they make up a Yiddishkeit both above and within understanding. He closes with blessings for the child and the family.

en: Every Jew has free choice, but he also carries a pintele Yid from the Avos that can never be extinguished.
This point of Avraham Avinu is above intellect, which is why even simple Jews give their lives for emunah.
Purim, when Jews reach 'until one does not know', reveals this point that is above daas.
Milah is done on a child without understanding because, as the bris of Avraham Avinu, it is above daas.
Tefillin, unlike milah, is a mitzvah bound up with daas.

title.en: Purim and the unquenchable point of Avraham

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that 'sasson' is milah and 'yikar' is tefillin, and explains that Purim reveals the hidden point of Avraham Avinu in every Jew, a pintele Yid above intellect that Hashem guards as 'Magen Avraham' and that shows itself in mesirus nefesh and in 'until one does not know'.

title.en: Milah above daas, tefillin with daas

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the great mitzvah of milah is done on an infant without understanding, and answers that as the bris of Avraham Avinu it is above daas, unlike tefillin, which is a mitzvah of daas. He closes with blessings for the child and the family.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Shushan Purim

oneLiner.en: At a bris seudah on Shushan Purim, the Mashgiach explains that Megillas Esther and Purim hold only a glimmer of the light of Moshiach, since the wiping out of Amalek is not yet complete, and that a bris milah, like Purim, removes the orlah and reveals that light.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara: Esther asked the Chachamim to write her book for all generations, and they answered that Amalek may be written only three times, not four. He asks why, and adds Shmuel's view that Esther is not one of the holy writings, though the twenty-four books are the ornaments of the Shechinah. He explains that every book existed in heaven before its navi wrote it; Megillas Esther holds a spark of the light of Moshiach, given to accustom the eyes, and Purim is not yet complete because Amalek is not yet wiped out. Bringing the Bnei Yissaschar and the Chasam Sofer, he links Purim to bris milah: both remove the orlah and reveal a glimpse of Moshiach. He applies this to the bris seudah on Shushan Purim, blesses the child and family, and closes by answering his opening question.

en: The Chachamim hesitated to write Megillas Esther because the Torah allows Amalek's war to be written three times, and a fourth time would require a complete wiping out of Amalek.
The twenty-four books of Tanach are the ornaments of the Shechinah, and each book existed in heaven before its navi drew it down into writing.
Megillas Esther and Purim hold a spark of the light of Moshiach, given so that Jews can grow used to that light before it comes in full.
Purim is not yet a finished yom tov, since its essence is the wiping out of Amalek, which is not yet complete.
A bris milah, like Purim, removes the orlah and reveals a glimpse of the days of Moshiach, so the Shushan Purim seudah is a seudah of bris milah.

title.en: Why Amalek may be written only three times

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Esther's request to be written for all generations and the Chachamim's answer that Amalek may be written only three times, and asks why. He adds Shmuel's view that Esther is not one of the holy writings, and asks how that fits with the twenty-four books corresponding to the twenty-four combinations of the Name Adnus.

title.en: The Megillah holds the light of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every navi's book existed in heaven before he wrote it, and that Megillas Esther holds a spark of the light of Moshiach, given to accustom Jews to that light. Since Purim's essence is the wiping out of Amalek, which is not yet complete, the Megillah's place among the holy writings is still hidden in heaven until Moshiach comes.

title.en: Purim, bris milah and the removal of the orlah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the Megillah has the laws of the holy writings only on Purim, and explains that on Purim Jews receive a glimpse of the days of Moshiach. He shows that a bris milah gives the same glimpse, brings the Chasam Sofer that 'Megillah' stands for removing idolatry from the land, and concludes that a Shushan Purim seudah is a seudah of bris milah.

title.en: A bris seudah on Shushan Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach says this bris seudah differs from others: on Shushan Purim every Jew who keeps Purim properly receives a measure of bris milah, is freed from his evil part, and can make a new covenant with Hashem. He praises the child's family of Torah, Chassidus and yiras Shamayim and blesses the child and the family to see the light of Moshiach.

title.en: Why the Chachamim finally wrote the Megillah

summary.en: After finishing his blessings, the Mashgiach returns to his opening question: Yehoshua, Shaul, and Mordechai and Esther each only weakened Amalek, and the Megillah, written in concealment without Hashem's name, shows the wiping out is not yet complete. The Chachamim wrote it once they understood that Hashem wanted Haman's descendants to learn Torah in Bnei Brak, and they were content with the glimpse of Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in Nissan, the Mashgiach links the removal of the orlah to the removal of chametz, which stands for the yetzer hara, and to the hope that Hashem will clear the world of evil.

abstract.en: Speaking at a bris held in the month of Nissan, the Mashgiach opens with the Haggadah's words about the son who asks, and speaks of Eliyahu HaNavi, who comes to the bris, in connection with questions and with the season of freedom. He then turns to chametz: it has many names, but they all point to one thing, the yetzer hara, the leaven in the dough. Milah, he says, carries the theme of Aleinu, removing impurity from the land and perfecting the world under the kingship of Hashem. This bris is no ordinary one: it falls in Nissan, when Jews are busy with biur chametz. Just as we search out and clear away our chametz, the Mashgiach asks that Hashem clear away the chametz and the yetzer hara from the whole world. He closes with brachos for the family and those honored at the bris, and for the zechus of Pesach and the korban Pesach.

en: Chametz has many names, but they all refer to one thing, the yetzer hara.
Milah carries the theme of Aleinu: removing impurity from the land and perfecting the world under Hashem's kingship.
A bris in Nissan, during biur chametz, calls for the prayer that Hashem clear the chametz and the yetzer hara from the world.

title.en: The son who asks and Eliyahu HaNavi

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Haggadah's words about the son who asks, and speaks of Eliyahu HaNavi in connection with questions and the time of freedom.

title.en: Chametz, the yetzer hara and milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that chametz stands for the yetzer hara and ties milah to Aleinu's hope of clearing impurity from the world. Since this bris falls during biur chametz, he asks that Hashem clear away the world's chametz, and closes with brachos for the family and for Pesach.

catalogTitle: תיקון לפגם הברית ע"י קר"ש שעל המטה. ביאור בהא דאין אומרים ברכה על דבר איסור.

oneLiner.en: Continuing Tanya chapters 7 and 8, the Mashgiach explains why the sin of wasted seed, though the gravest, can be repaired through teshuvah and Krias Shema at bedtime, and why no brachah is made on forbidden food.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews which energies can be elevated and turns to the sin the Shulchan Aruch calls the worst, wasted seed, whose repair is nevertheless close at hand. He explains that both kedushah and klipah have a male and female side, illustrated by the Names Havayah and Adnus, by the numerical value of Amen, and by Yaakov's gift of 580 animals to Esav. Wasted seed is influence without a receiver, so it can be gathered back. In the Sitra Achra the female side is the stronger, which he shows from the Ohr HaChaim's dream and from Rashi on Esav, and he digresses on how the nations follow their angel's left-sided order. He then shows that the repair comes through teshuvah and Krias Shema at bedtime, contrasts forbidden relations and a mamzer, speaks of Hashem's ways above the order of judgment, and explains every sin as separation. He closes with Tanya chapter 8 and the Tzemach Tzedek's reason that no brachah is made on forbidden food.

en: Wasted seed is the gravest sin, yet its repair is accessible even now, without waiting for the days of Moshiach or for teshuvah out of love.
Every flow of bounty, in kedushah and in the Sitra Achra alike, needs a giver and a receiver, a male and a female aspect.
Because wasted seed is influence without a receiver, the holy energy thrown to impurity was not absorbed and can be gathered back to kedushah.
The repair comes through teshuvah and Krias Shema at bedtime, which the Mashgiach calls the weakest of the daily recitals of Shema and yet the strongest.
Forbidden relations are harder to repair, because the energy is held by the female side of the klipah; a mamzer cannot be undone by the mechanics of teshuvah.
The essence of every sin is separation from Hashem's oneness, and the repair of tumas keri is to believe that nothing is mere chance.
Following the Tzemach Tzedek, the Mashgiach explains that no brachah is made on forbidden food because a brachah elevates the holy sparks in food, and forbidden food has no ascent.

title.en: Review, and the gravest sin

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the previous week: energy from permitted food can later be elevated, while energy from forbidden food cannot. He then introduces wasted seed, called in Shulchan Aruch Even HaEzer the worst sin, whose repair is nevertheless available right away.

title.en: Male and female in kedushah and klipah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that kedushah has a male aspect, the Name Havayah, and a female aspect, the Name Adnus, whose union is alluded to in Amen; the Sitra Achra has its counterparts. He shows that Yaakov's 580 animals sent to Esav match the numerical value of Esav's force and neutralized it.

title.en: Influence without a receiver

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in all forbidden relations there is a giver and a receiver, but wasted seed has no receiver, so it can be gathered back. He tells the Ohr HaChaim's dream of two dogs to show that in the Sitra Achra the female is stronger, and brings Rashi on Esav placing his wives first.

title.en: The nations, their angel, and the left side

summary.en: The Mashgiach digresses: each of the seventy nations is guided by its angel, so the nations put the female first, button left over right and write from left to right, while Jews do the opposite. The Arabs, the refuse of Avraham's chesed, write from right to left and keep a purely lunar calendar, while Jews blend moon and sun with a leap month.

title.en: Teshuvah and Krias Shema at bedtime

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the Tanya: wasted seed can be gathered back through teshuvah and Krias Shema at bedtime, the weakest and strongest of the daily Shemas. He notes the Torah never writes it as an explicit prohibition, bringing Rav Tzadok's reason that it is often involuntary, and explains the Gemara that Krias Shema at bedtime is like a double-edged sword against the harmful forces clothed in those drops.

title.en: Forbidden relations and a mamzer

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that forbidden relations strengthen the klipah more, since the energy is held by its female side, and ordinary teshuvah does not help unless it turns sins into merits. A mamzer cannot be repaired by the mechanics of teshuvah, though the seforim hakedoshim say that through a great teshuvah the mamzer dies and the repair is complete.

title.en: Hashem's ways above the order of judgment

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the mamzer's death as a release for the suffering neshamah, like a neshamah in a cat, and answers a listener about the future. He then says Hashem is not bound by the order of judgment: at times He purifies a mamzer and keeps him alive, Moshiach comes from such a line, and He will bring the geulah even without teshuvah.

title.en: Every sin is separation

summary.en: Answering a question, the Mashgiach explains that the essence of every sin is separation, as in 'yispardu kol po'alei aven', and that division was created on the second day. Amalek's tumas keri means chance, and he brings Rav Tzadok that its repair is to believe in Hashem's oneness, that nothing simply happens.

title.en: Tanya chapter 8: no brachah on forbidden food

summary.en: Beginning chapter 8, the Mashgiach explains that forbidden food eaten unknowingly for the sake of Heaven still has no ascent, even a rabbinic prohibition. He brings the Tzemach Tzedek that this is why no brachah is made on it, with the Gemara on stolen wheat, the Bnei Yissaschar's inquiry on the brachah over the mann, and the Taz who differs.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - RCH Nissan

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, the Mashgiach presents the bris as a foretaste of the days of Moshiach and sees this day, and this year's calendar, as a special opening for the Geulah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by describing a bris as a kind of preview of the revelation of Moshiach: the orlah is removed, recalling the hope of removing impurity from the land and perfecting the world under Hashem's kingship. He cites the Lubliner on the bris as a glimpse of the days of Moshiach, and notes that the Harachaman prayers at a bris mention Eliyahu HaNavi and Moshiach. He then turns to the day: Rosh Chodesh Nissan took ten crowns, among them being the first day of creation, and this year it fell on Sunday. He adds that a year in which Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos is described as a great sign for Moshiach's coming, so this simcha can help bring the Geulah awaited by all the worlds. He closes by praising the family, recalling an elder of the family, Reb Yechezkel, a great talmid chacham, and blessing the child.

en: A bris is a preview of the revelation of Moshiach, and the removal of the orlah recalls the hope of removing impurity from the world.
Rosh Chodesh Nissan took ten crowns, one being the first day of creation, and this year it fell on Sunday.
A year in which Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos is described as a great sign for the coming of Moshiach.
This simcha can help bring the Geulah that all the upper and lower worlds await.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Korban Nasi Dan

oneLiner.en: At a bris on the day of the korban of the Nasi of Dan, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem takes pride in Dan, the last tribe, as in the last generation of galus, and that the child brought to the bris is a korban before the Shechinah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the day's reading of the korban of Achiezer ben Ammishaddai, the Nasi of the tribe of Dan, and the Midrash on Hashem's words 'this is the korban'. Dan was a lowly tribe, some of whose people were cast out and exposed to Amalek in war, yet Hashem made a special yom tov for each tribe, and today is the yom tov of Dan. Dan traveled last, gathering in all the camps, and the Mashgiach sees in this the end of galus: we, at the end of the exile, are in the period of Dan, and Hashem rejoices and boasts of us before the angels. Chazal liken bringing a child to his bris to bringing a korban, so the child is offered before the Shechinah. The last generation, the heel before Moshiach, will be the greatest of all generations, greater even than the generation of Yetzias Mitzrayim. He closes by blessing the child to grow in Torah and good deeds, and the parents and grandparents with nachas.

en: Hashem made a special yom tov for each tribe through its Nasi's korban, and today is the yom tov of the tribe of Dan.
Dan, which traveled last and gathered in all the camps, corresponds to the end of galus, the time we are in.
Chazal liken bringing a child to his bris to bringing a korban, so the child is offered before the Shechinah.
The last generation, the heel before Moshiach, will be the greatest of all, greater than the generation of Yetzias Mitzrayim.

title.en: The korban of Dan and the last generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the korban of Achiezer ben Ammishaddai, the Nasi of Dan: Dan was a lowly tribe and traveled last, like us at the end of galus, yet Hashem boasts of it, and the child at the bris is a korban before the Shechinah. The last generation, he says, will be the greatest, and he closes with brachos for the child and family.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Erev Pesach

oneLiner.en: At a bris just before Pesach, the Mashgiach connects the child's entry into the covenant with Eliyahu Hanavi, who is present at the bris, announced on Shabbos Hagadol and awaited at the Seder, and with the rule that the Korban Pesach requires milah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach speaks at a bris shortly before Pesach. He notes that Chazal say Eliyahu Hanavi comes to every bris, that on Shabbos Hagadol the haftarah announces 'Behold I send you Eliyahu the prophet', and that Jews hold that Eliyahu comes to every Jewish home at the Seder. A bris within these few days thus joins Eliyahu, the bearer of good tidings, three times over, and the Mashgiach calls it a good sign for the child. He blesses that Eliyahu, of whom it is said that the covenant was with him for life and peace, bring peace and the redemption, and that this seemingly private family simcha be the spark that ignites his coming. He then explains that milah is a central preparation for Pesach, since the Korban Pesach cannot be offered without it, and blesses that the child bring redemption to himself and to all of Klal Yisrael.

en: A bris just before Pesach links the child with Eliyahu Hanavi, who comes to the bris, is announced on Shabbos Hagadol and comes to the Seder.
The Mashgiach calls it a good sign that the child entered the covenant of Avraham Avinu at a time when everyone awaits Eliyahu, the bearer of good tidings.
He asks that this family bris, seemingly a private matter, be the spark that ignites the coming of Eliyahu and the redemption.
Milah is one of the most important preparations for Pesach, since the Korban Pesach cannot be offered without it.

catalogTitle: הסבר על מה שקורא התניא למצוות דרבנן דברי סופרים. חילוק בין שידין נוכראין ושידין יהודאין. עונש דברים בטלים' ומאכלי תאווה.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Tanya calls rabbinic laws 'divrei soferim', how the Chachamim saw the root of every letter of the Torah, and then the Tanya's distinction between non-Jewish and Jewish shedim and the punishments for forbidden food, food of desire and idle talk.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that the Tanya treats a rabbinic prohibition as coming from the klipos, and that it calls the Rabbis 'soferim', after the Gemara that the early sages counted the letters of the Torah. To them every letter was a 'davar shebeminyan', something important in itself, because they saw the root of the Torah; Rabbi Akiva expounded even the crowns of the letters, and Rabbi Meir could write a Megillah by heart because he copied from the Torah's root in heaven. From there he speaks of tzaddikim who read the Torah in the world itself, and of turning the ayin of 'kosnos or' and of the forest swine into an aleph. Returning to Tanya chapter eight, he explains the two kinds of shedim, the severity of chalav akum, two stories about it, and the punishments the sefarim describe for food eaten from desire and for idle talk.

en: The Mashgiach explains that the Tanya holds a rabbinic prohibition draws its life from the klipah, and that the Rabbis know this because they see into the root of things.
He teaches that to the Chachamim each single letter of the Torah was a 'davar shebeminyan', a thing of importance, because every letter taught them new halachos.
Rabbi Meir could write a Megillah by heart because he saw the Torah's root in heaven and was in effect copying from a written text.
The Mashgiach describes the Jew's task as turning the ayin into an aleph: seeing the Master of the world inside what looks like impurity, which sweetens it.

Shedim nukhraim are the desire for forbidden things, while shedim yehudaim are a desire for permitted things that are not needed; the latter can be raised back to holiness through teshuvah or through using the strength for Torah and avodah.
Food eaten only for pleasure leaves a residue even when its strength is used for learning, and the sefarim describe a purging in the grave for it; idle talk brings a different, lighter punishment.

title.en: Why rabbinic laws are 'divrei soferim'

summary.en: After a quick review of the text, the Mashgiach notes that the Tanya treats a rabbinic prohibition as coming from the klipah, stresses how precise the Tanya is in every word, and brings the Gemara that the early sages were called soferim because they counted the letters. He introduces the idea of a 'davar shebeminyan', using potatoes and oranges to explain it.

title.en: Every letter is a root

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that ordinary learning needs a phrase that carries a thought, while the Chachamim expounded single letters, and Rabbi Akiva even the crowns on the letters. A letter teaches as the root of a tree feeds its fruit, and the Chachamim could see everything contained in that root.

title.en: Rabbi Meir and reading the Torah in the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that a Sefer Torah may not be written by heart, and asks how Rabbi Meir wrote a Megillah by heart; he answers that Rabbi Meir saw the Torah's root in heaven. Since the world was created through the Torah, tzaddikim could read the Torah in the world, and he tells of a tzaddik who looked at a cut apple every motzaei Shabbos.

title.en: Turning the ayin into an aleph

summary.en: From the garments of skin given to Adam and Chava, the Mashgiach explains that the inner point was 'or' with an aleph, light, and that a Jew's work is to turn the ayin into an aleph. He applies this to the suspended ayin in 'chazir miyaar' and to the middle of Tehillim, where the impure can become pure, after a disclaimer that he speaks of matters above his own level.

title.en: Shedim and refined speech

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the Tanya: the Rabbis see the root, so they know a rabbinic prohibition comes from the klipos. He reads the Tanya's words that a desire for forbidden food is a shed of the non-Jewish shedim, and explains why refined Jews avoid saying the word 'shed' and speak in refined language, because what a person says is drawn upon him.

title.en: Non-Jewish and Jewish shedim; the Russian censor

summary.en: The Mashgiach defines the two kinds: the shedim nukhraim stir a desire for what is forbidden, while the shedim yehudaim stir a desire for something kosher but unnecessary. Noting that the passage was altered by the censor, he digresses on how Russian censors changed words in seforim, Gemaras and siddurim.

title.en: Why chalav akum is worse than chazir

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a desire from the shedim yehudaim can return to holiness through teshuvah or through Torah and avodah, while the shedim nukhraim reach the root of the goy. Therefore chalav akum is in one sense worse than chazir, and he brings the Tzemach Tzedek that chalav akum, chametz on Pesach and niddah touch that root and can block a Jew's readiness for mesiras nefesh.

title.en: The old wine merchant in Tosafos

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that in recent generations people who ate these things lost their readiness for mesiras nefesh. He brings Tosafos' story of an old man who drank wine a goy had touched only to cause him a loss, relying on the ruling that this is not yayin nesech, and who was later killed; the Mashgiach explains that his death al kiddush Hashem showed his ruling was correct.

title.en: Chalav akum, doubts in emunah, and Rav Moshe's milk

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a man who complained to the Ba'al HaTanya about doubts in emunah and was told it came from drinking chalav akum. He mentions the dispute over supervised milk in America and tells how Rav Moshe Feinstein, who was lenient for others, vomited up milk without a hechsher served to him. He adds that teshuvah helps, yet until then the thing still tilts toward the other side.

title.en: The residue of food eaten from desire

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that food eaten only for enjoyment leaves a residue even if one then learns with its strength, comparing it to dust on a mattress that must be beaten out; the musar sefarim call this the beating in the grave, while forbidden food is a real stain that needs the laundering of Gehinnom. Only someone like Rebbi, who had no pleasure from this world, is spared, and he tells of a tzaddik who made a siyum every day so that every meal was a seudas mitzvah.

title.en: The punishment for idle talk

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes a lighter punishment the sefarim give for idle talk, in which the soul is thrown back and forth. He distinguishes the talmid chacham, who is asked why he did not speak words of Torah, from the am haaretz, who is asked why he enjoyed this world, which was made only for the service of Hashem.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Pesach, the Mashgiach explains that Pesach, the head of the Yamim Tovim, binds Klal Yisrael to Hashem, that milah is a bond of its own, and that a bris on Pesach, with Eliyahu Hanavi present at both, is a bond upon a bond.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Rambam in Sefer Hamitzvos: the month can be sanctified only in Eretz Yisrael, so without Jews settled there there would be no Yamim Tovim, and that would be the destruction of Klal Yisrael. The three Regalim are thus the existence of the nation, and Pesach is the head of them all. Citing the Chiddushei HaRim, he explains that Pesach alone carries kareis, for chametz and for not bringing the Korban Pesach, a sign that its mitzvos bind Jews to Hashem; and eating the Korban Pesach requires milah, another bond. Milah too carries kareis, so a bris on Pesach is a bond upon a bond. Eliyahu Hanavi, who turns the hearts of fathers to sons, comes both at Pesach and at a bris, and hearing good tidings is a time of favor for renewal. He closes with blessings for the redemption.

en: According to the Rambam, the Yamim Tovim depend on sanctifying the month in Eretz Yisrael, and the three Regalim are the existence of Klal Yisrael.
Pesach is the head of all the Yamim Tovim and establishes the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael.
The kareis attached to Pesach's mitzvos shows that they bind a Jew to Hashem, and milah, required for the Korban Pesach, is a further bond.
A bris on Pesach is a bond upon a bond, and Eliyahu Hanavi, who binds Jews to Hashem, comes to both.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Chol Hamoed Pesach, the Mashgiach explains that milah, the removal of the orlah, is a person's own removal of chametz and a model of the removal of impurity from the world that Pesach and the days of Moshiach bring.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that Pesach is a time of Eliyahu Hanavi, announced on Shabbos Hagadol, when Jews await the great salvation. Pesach nullifies the kelipos, the forces of evil, through removing chametz, and a person's own removal is the bris milah that removes the orlah; the Torah requires milah to eat the Korban Pesach. Each bris awakens the days of Moshiach and is a model of removing the spirit of impurity from the land. Avraham Avinu's war with the four kings on Pesach, he says, was against the four layers of the orlah, the four kelipos. Pesach and milah are the only positive mitzvos carrying kareis, and the Chiddushei HaRim says the reverse of kareis is a bond with Hashem, so a bris on Pesach is especially in its time. He explains why Aleinu is said after a bris, and closes with blessings.

en: Pesach nullifies the kelipos through removing chametz, and bris milah, removing the orlah, is a person's own removal.
Every bris awakens the days of Moshiach and is a model of removing the spirit of impurity from the land.
Avraham Avinu's war with the four kings on Pesach corresponds to the four layers of the orlah, the four kelipos.
Pesach and milah alone among positive mitzvos carry kareis, and since the reverse of kareis is a bond with Hashem, a bris on Pesach is especially in its time.

title.en: Milah as removing the orlah on Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the bris to the removal of chametz, explains that milah is a model of removing impurity from the world and ties the four layers of the orlah to Avraham Avinu's war with the four kings on Pesach. From the kareis shared by Pesach and milah he concludes that a bris on Pesach is especially in its time, explains why Aleinu is said after a bris, and closes with blessings.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shavuos is fixed by the counting of every Jew rather than by Beis Din's calendar, because every Jew holds the Torah as an inheritance and can become a great talmid chacham, and he blesses the child at the bris to realize that potential.

abstract.en: At a bris during Sefirah, the Mashgiach notes that the other festivals depend on Beis Din, on the sanctifying of the month and the leap year. Shavuos alone has no fixed date; it falls fifty days after Pesach, set by the counting. Following the Chasam Sofer, he asks why the Torah tied Shavuos to counting. He answers that every Jew holds the Torah as an inheritance in his soul, so even a simple Jew carries the potential to be, or to raise, a great talmid chacham. Since every Jew counts, every Jew fixes the day of the giving of the Torah, showing that each is a 'master of the house' in Torah. He connects this to the bris, where the child receives the powers of his soul, and blesses him to grow into a great talmid chacham and to receive the Torah on Shavuos.

en: Shavuos is fixed by counting fifty days from Pesach, not by a calendar date set through Beis Din's sanctifying of the month.
Every Jew holds the Torah as an inheritance in his soul, so every Jew carries the potential of a talmid chacham.
Because the counting belongs to every single Jew, every Jew takes part in fixing the time of the giving of the Torah.
At the bris the child receives the powers of his soul, which he can develop into greatness in Torah and yiras Shamayim.

title.en: Shavuos fixed by everyone's counting, and the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the festivals fixed by Beis Din's sanctifying of the month with Shavuos, which falls fifty days after Pesach by the counting, and asks with the Chasam Sofer why. He answers that every Jew inherits the Torah and carries the potential of a great talmid chacham, so every Jew, by counting, fixes the day of the giving of the Torah. He then applies this to the bris and blesses the child to grow into a great talmid chacham and receive the Torah on Shavuos.
